purpose: Nortriptyline is mainly used to treat depression, but doctors also prescribe it for nerve pain, migraines, and sometimes to help people quit smoking. It can help lift your mood, improve sleep, and increase your energy levels. Your doctor may also use it for other conditions not listed here.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called serotonin and norepinephrine to help regulate your mood and how you feel pain. Nortriptyline works by keeping more of these chemicals available in your brain for longer. This helps improve communication between brain cells, which over time helps relieve depression and reduce pain signals.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, feeling drowsy or dizzy, weight gain, difficulty urinating, and increased sweating are common. You may also notice your heart beating faster than usual. Many of these effects are more noticeable when you first start the medication and may improve over time.
warnings: Do not suddenly stop taking this medication without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. It can increase thoughts of suicide especially in children, teens, and young adults, so report any worsening mood changes right away. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, glaucoma, seizures, or if you are taking other medications, since nortriptyline can interact with many drugs. Do not take it within 14 days of taking an MAO inhibitor.
typical_dosing: Adults typically start at 25 mg taken one to four times a day, and the dose is gradually increased as needed up to about 150 mg per day. Older adults usually start on a lower dose, around 10 to 25 mg at bedtime. It can take 2 to 4 weeks before you notice the full benefit, so be patient and keep taking it as directed.
